questions.question: In object-oriented programming, what does abstraction mean?
options: Hiding an object's data behind access modifiers and exposing it only through getters and setters
Hiding the implementation details (the bodies) of methods and showing only their method signatures
Reusing the fields and methods of a parent class inside a child class
Splitting a program into packages so that classes cannot see each other's source code
questions.explanation: Abstraction hides how a method works (its body) and exposes only what it offers (its signature). Hiding data behind access modifiers and getters/setters is encapsulation, a different OOP pillar.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes abstraction from encapsulation?
options: Abstraction hides method implementation using abstract classes and interfaces; encapsulation hides data using access modifiers with getters and setters
Abstraction hides data using access modifiers; encapsulation hides method implementation using interfaces
They are two interchangeable names for exactly the same technique
Abstraction applies only to variables, while encapsulation applies only to methods
questions.explanation: Both pillars hide something, but the targets differ: abstraction hides implementation (method bodies) via abstract classes and interfaces, while encapsulation hides state (data) via access modifiers, getters and setters.

questions.question: To drive a car you use only the pedals, gear shift and steering wheel, and you never see how the engine works. In abstraction terms, what do the pedals and wheel represent?
options: The implementation, because they are the parts that physically make the car move
Encapsulated private data belonging to the car
The exposed interface (the contract) through which the hidden implementation is used
An abstract method, because the driver must supply their own body for it
questions.explanation: The controls are the simple interface the driver depends on, while the engine and transmission are the hidden implementation. Abstraction means using something through its contract without ever seeing the machinery underneath.

questions.question: Which two Java constructs are the main tools for achieving abstraction?
options: Getters and setters
Constructors and method overloading
Packages and access modifiers
Abstract classes and interfaces
questions.explanation: Java implements abstraction through the abstract keyword (abstract classes and abstract methods) and through interfaces, which are fully abstract contracts. Getters, setters and access modifiers are the tools of encapsulation instead.

questions.question: What happens if code tries to create an object of an abstract class directly with new?
options: It compiles, but an exception is thrown at run time
An object is created whose abstract methods simply do nothing
The code fails to compile
It compiles with a warning and the nearest concrete subclass is instantiated instead
questions.explanation: Declaring a class abstract imposes a compile-time rule: it can never be instantiated, only inherited. The compiler rejects any new expression on an abstract class.

questions.question: How is an abstract method written inside an abstract class?
options: A method signature followed by empty braces { }
A method signature ending in a semicolon, with no body at all
A full method whose body simply returns a default value
A method marked final so that subclasses are forced to replace its body
questions.explanation: An abstract method supplies only the signature: instead of a { } body it ends with a semicolon, with the abstract keyword placed after the access modifier and before the return type. Empty braces would be a concrete method with an empty body, which is different.

questions.question: Which keyword does a class use to declare that it will fulfil an interface's contract?
options: extends
interface
abstract
implements
questions.explanation: A class implements an interface; classes use extends only for inheriting another class. Interfaces themselves use extends when they inherit other interfaces.

questions.question: How many classes can a Java class extend, and how many interfaces can it implement?
options: It can extend at most one class but implement many interfaces
It can extend many classes but implement only one interface
It can extend at most one class and implement at most one interface
It can extend many classes and implement many interfaces
questions.explanation: Java allows single inheritance of classes (extends exactly one) but multiple inheritance of type through interfaces (implements as many as needed). Needing behaviour from multiple sources is a key reason to choose interfaces.

questions.question: Which pairing of relationships is correct?
options: Interface: is-a relationship; abstract class: can-do relationship
Both abstract classes and interfaces express only is-a relationships
Abstract class: is-a relationship; interface: can-do relationship (a capability)
Both abstract classes and interfaces express only can-do relationships
questions.explanation: Extending an abstract class says what the object is (a Dog is an Animal), while implementing an interface says what it can do (a Bird can fly, so it implements Flyable). This distinction guides which construct to choose in a design.

questions.question: What is the result of compiling and running this code?
options: It prints nothing and exits normally
It throws an exception at run time when play() is called
It compiles only if play() is given a default body
It fails to compile: an interface cannot be instantiated
questions.explanation: Interfaces are pure contracts and can never be instantiated with new; they can only be implemented by classes or extended by other interfaces. Only a concrete implementing class could be instantiated and assigned to a Playable variable.

questions.question: A class contains one abstract method and nine ordinary methods with bodies. What does the compiler require?
options: The class itself must be declared abstract
Nothing extra: only classes where every method is abstract need the abstract keyword
The class must be converted into an interface
The other nine methods must also be declared abstract
questions.explanation: Even a single abstract method makes the class incomplete, so the class must be declared abstract. Abstract classes may freely mix abstract methods with concrete ones.

questions.question: Does this code compile?
options: Yes: Triangle inherits area() and may leave it unimplemented
No: Triangle must implement area() or be declared abstract itself
No: an abstract class may not contain an abstract method
Yes, but calling area() on a Triangle throws an exception at run time
questions.explanation: A subclass that inherits an abstract method has exactly two options: provide a body for it, or be declared abstract and pass the obligation on. Triangle does neither, so compilation fails.

questions.question: Does this hierarchy compile?
options: No: B must implement m() because it extends A
No: an abstract class cannot extend another abstract class
Yes: B stays abstract so it may leave m() unimplemented, and C finally provides the body
Yes, but only C is usable; A and B are removed by the compiler
questions.explanation: An abstract subclass may leave inherited abstract methods unimplemented and pass them down. The chain is legal because some descendant (here C) eventually implements everything; otherwise the family could never produce a single object.

questions.question: What is the result of this code?
options: It prints Braking...
It compiles because Vehicle has no abstract methods, but crashes at run time
It prints nothing
It fails to compile: Vehicle is abstract, even though it contains no abstract methods
questions.explanation: An abstract class may contain zero abstract methods; the abstract keyword on the class declaration alone forbids instantiation. Whether new is allowed depends on how the class is declared, not on what it contains.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: It prints "I am Spot" then "Woof!"
It fails to compile: an abstract class cannot have a constructor
It fails to compile: makeSound() cannot be called through an Animal reference
It prints "I am Spot" then fails at run time because Animal has no makeSound() body
questions.explanation: Abstract classes can have constructors (run through super()) and an Animal reference may hold a Dog object. Calling makeSound() through the Animal type is legal and dynamically runs Dog's implementation, so both lines print.

questions.question: Can an abstract class declare a constructor?
options: No: since it cannot be instantiated, a constructor would be meaningless
Yes: subclasses call it with super() to initialise the inherited part of the object
Only if the class contains no abstract methods
Yes, but the constructor must be declared abstract as well
questions.explanation: Abstract classes can hold state, so they have constructors to initialise it; subclass constructors invoke them via super(), never via new. Interfaces, by contrast, have no constructors at all.

questions.question: Inside an interface, a method is declared as: void method1(); Which modifiers does it implicitly have?
options: package-private and abstract
protected and abstract
public and abstract
public and final
questions.explanation: All ordinary method declarations in an interface are implicitly public abstract, so writing void method1(); and public abstract void method1(); mean exactly the same thing. Interface methods are never package-private or protected.

questions.question: Inside an interface, a variable is declared as: double PI = 3.1415; Which modifiers does it implicitly have?
options: private static final
public abstract
protected static
public static final
questions.explanation: Every variable declared in an interface is implicitly public static final, making it a constant shared by all implementers. That is why it must be initialised where declared and can never be reassigned.

questions.question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: Dog is missing the @Override annotation, which is mandatory when implementing an interface
Interface methods are implicitly public, and Dog's speak() has weaker (package-private) access; an implementation may not reduce access
Dog must also extend a class before it may implement an interface
speak() in the interface needs a body before Dog can implement it
questions.explanation: The interface's speak() is implicitly public, but Dog's version has default (package-private) access, and Java never lets an implementing method weaken access. The fix is to declare it public void speak(); @Override is helpful but optional.

questions.question: Vehicle is an abstract class; Car is a concrete class extending Vehicle; Circle is a concrete class implementing the Drawable interface and its draw() prints a message. Which lines compile?
questions.code:
Vehicle v = new Vehicle();   // line 1
Vehicle c = new Car();       // line 2
Drawable d = new Circle();   // line 3
d.draw();                    // line 4
options: Lines 2, 3 and 4 only
All four lines
Lines 3 and 4 only
Line 2 only
questions.explanation: Line 1 fails because an abstract class can never be instantiated. A parent-type or interface-type reference may hold any concrete implementer, so lines 2 and 3 are fine, and calling draw() through the interface reference on line 4 is exactly how interfaces are meant to be used.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Nothing: an interface reference cannot invoke methods
It fails to compile because a variable's type may not be an interface
Drawing a circle
It fails to compile because Circle should use extends, not implements
questions.explanation: An interface is a valid reference type: the variable is typed by the contract while the object supplies the implementation. The call d.draw() runs Circle's method and prints Drawing a circle.

questions.question: Which list contains only things an interface may contain (Java 8 and later)?
options: Method signatures, constructors and instance variables
Only method signatures: nothing else is permitted
Constants, method signatures and constructors
Constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods and nested types
questions.explanation: An interface may hold constants, abstract method signatures, default and static methods (since Java 8) and nested types. It can never contain constructors or instance variables; its variables are implicitly public static final constants.

questions.question: Since Java 8, which interface methods are allowed to have a body?
options: None: every interface method must be a bare signature
default methods and static methods
Any method, as long as it is declared protected
Only methods explicitly marked abstract
questions.explanation: Java 8 added default and static methods, which carry implementations inside the interface itself. Ordinary interface methods remain implicitly abstract signatures, and an abstract method by definition has no body.

questions.question: Does this code compile?
options: Yes: a class may implement any number of interfaces, provided it implements all their methods
No: a class may implement only one interface at a time
No: Smartwatch must use extends for the first interface and implements for the second
Only if Wearable and Chargeable extend a common parent interface
questions.explanation: Multiple interfaces are listed after implements, separated by commas; this is Java's multiple inheritance of type. Smartwatch honours both contracts by giving every declared method a public implementation.

questions.question: Closely related classes Dog, Cat and Horse all need the same name and age fields, a shared sleep() method with a body, and each needs its own makeSound(). A generic "animal" should never be created directly. What is the best design?
options: An Animal interface that Dog, Cat and Horse implement
A concrete Animal superclass that is instantiated whenever a generic animal is needed
An abstract Animal class holding the fields and sleep(), with makeSound() declared abstract
Three unrelated classes, each duplicating the fields and the sleep() method
questions.explanation: Shared state (instance fields) and shared method bodies among close relatives point to an abstract class, because interfaces cannot hold instance variables. Declaring Animal abstract also guarantees no generic animal is ever instantiated.

questions.question: Bird, Airplane and Superman are unrelated classes in different hierarchies, but each must offer a fly() behaviour. What is the best design?
options: Make them all extend an abstract Flyer class that declares fly()
Give each class its own unrelated fly() method and cast between the types as needed
Pick one of the three classes as the parent and have the other two extend it
Define a Flyable interface with fly() and have each class implement it
questions.explanation: A capability shared by unrelated classes is exactly what interfaces are for: any class, anywhere in any hierarchy, can implement Flyable. A common superclass cannot work here because each class may already have its own parent and Java allows only single inheritance.

questions.question: What is the result of this code?
options: It fails to compile: MAX is implicitly final and cannot be reassigned
It prints 20
It prints 10 because the assignment is silently ignored
It fails to compile: interface variables can only ever be accessed as Config.MAX
questions.explanation: Interface variables are implicitly public static final, so MAX is a constant and assigning to it is a compile-time error. Reading it unqualified from an implementing class would be perfectly legal; it is the assignment that breaks the code.

questions.question: What is the result of this code?
options: It fails to compile: Radio must implement pause() as well
It prints "Playing radio" then "Paused"
It fails to compile: interface methods can never have bodies
It prints "Playing radio" then throws an exception because Radio has no pause()
questions.explanation: A default method (Java 8+) ships a ready-made body with the interface, so implementers only have to supply the abstract methods, here just play(). Radio inherits pause() from the interface and the call prints Paused.

questions.question: A NotificationManager class depends only on a MessageService interface. Adding a brand-new EmailService implementation requires no change to NotificationManager. Which principle does this illustrate, and why?
options: Encapsulation, because the manager's fields are private so new services cannot corrupt them
Single inheritance, because each service extends exactly one manager
Method overloading, because the manager gains a new sendNotification variant for each service
The Open/Closed Principle: the system is open to extension through new implementations but closed to modification of existing client code
questions.explanation: Open/Closed says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Because the client codes against the stable interface contract, new implementers can be added at any time while the existing client code stays untouched.

questions.question: Does this code compile?
options: Yes: one add method is enough to satisfy the contract
Yes: add(int) overloads add(int, int), and overloads count as implementations
No: Basic never implements add(int, int); an implementing method must match the interface's signature exactly
No: methods in an implementing class may not be overloaded
questions.explanation: A class must implement every abstract method with the exact signature (name and parameters) declared in the interface. add(int) is a different method, an overload, so the add(int, int) contract remains unfulfilled and Basic fails to compile as a concrete class.

questions.question: Given interface A, interface B and class C, which of these declarations is legal?
options: interface B implements A
interface B extends A
interface B extends C
class C extends A
questions.explanation: An interface may extend other interfaces, but it never implements anything and never inherits from a class. A class, in turn, must use implements (not extends) to adopt an interface.

questions.question: A method is declared as sendNotification(MessageService service, String msg), where MessageService is an interface. What is the main benefit of typing the parameter by the interface?
options: Any present or future implementation (SMS, WhatsApp, Email, ...) can be passed in without changing the method
The method runs faster because interface calls skip dynamic dispatch
The method can create its own MessageService instances with new whenever it needs one
Implementations passed to it are excused from implementing the interface's other methods
questions.explanation: Programming to an interface means the method depends only on the contract, so every implementer, including ones written later, is accepted automatically. This keeps code flexible and reusable and is the mechanism behind the Open/Closed Principle.
